item.title: Pets.com died, Amazon survived. What the 2000 bubble says about AI services
item.description:
On March 10, 2000, the NASDAQ index reached its peak. By the fall of 2002, it had lost almost 78%. Pets.com went public in February 2000 and was already selling off its assets by November of the same year. Webvan, a grocery delivery service with a billion-dollar valuation, went bankrupt in the summer of 2001. Amazon's stock fell by more than 90% over the same two years, but the company survived. The survivors weren't those with the best websites. Pets.com had a great website and advertising; its sock puppet mascot is still remembered today. But under the website, they had nothing of their own: they bought pet food from the same suppliers as regular pet stores and sold it below cost. Amazon, meanwhile, was building warehouses and logistics that couldn't be replicated overnight. The same is happening with AI services now. Most are set up the same way: a form on a website, a prompt, a request to someone else's neural network, and an answer on the screen. As soon as the neural network owner adds such a feature themselves, the service loses its meaning. This already happened with "chat with PDF" services when file uploads were added to the chatbots themselves. Since May, I've been developing a contract review service, and during this time, I've compiled a list for myself: what an AI service needs to be trusted with work, not just for play. The examples in it are from contracts, but the rules, in my opinion, are applicable to any industry. Read more

item.title: CLI Harness. Management via Telegram. Claude, GPT, and Qwen in a single terminal agent built on pi
item.description:
We tested how the agent edits files in 250 team sessions. It wrote to files via shell about 590 times, even though it had edit and write tools. 442 of these writes were due to a single phrase in one skill. We've accumulated many such stories during Veai CLI development. Veai CLI works in the terminal, like Claude Code and Codex. Its first public version is out today. Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, DeepSeek, GLM, and Qwen models are available through it with a single subscription and without a VPN, and you can pay with a Russian card. First, we'll explain who needs Veai CLI, what it can do, and how it differs from Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and Koda CLI. Then, in the "Under the Hood" section, we'll explain how it's built and what challenges we faced. Pricing and installation are at the end of the article. Read on

item.title: Why "Vibe Coding" Isn't for All Developers
item.description:
For almost a year now, AI has been not an experiment for me, but a working tool: real projects, real deadlines, real responsibility for the result. And over this year, I've seen that people who "write code with AI" do it fundamentally differently. Some throw a prompt and take what comes out. Others design a system where AI does the work under their control. Andrey Karpaty, who coined the term "vibe coding" in February 2025, meant something simple: to whip up a business card website or a utility for oneself, without reading the code, trusting the result. But the word stuck to everything: from crafts to production systems where an engineer is responsible for every line. The difference between these two ways of working is huge, and a name for the second approach seems to be missing. On top of that, many truly abuse the technology and create quick, unverified solutions targeting responsible niches where they show their weakness, lack of refinement, and data security threats. Such solutions have added a negative connotation to the concept of "vibe coding," and real software engineers have inadvertently been lumped in with beginners and received the "shameful" label of vibe coder. This situation seemed unfair to me, not because engineers might be offended, but because there's a substitution of concepts, and a misconception on the business side when evaluating the product being created. Businesses in production don't need MVPs and "one-evening" crafts; they need an architecturally strong and reliable product for which the developer is responsible and provides guarantees. Therefore, defining the concepts became a concrete task for me to form a domain and a common language for communication in the IT environment. Read more

item.title: Recruiter Bots, ATS, and Auto-Filters: Can You Reach a Human Today?
item.description:
An email arrived for Alexander at night, starting with: 'Hello, [Name]!' The script failed to insert the name, leaving the brackets intact, despite it being in his resume. It then asked him to answer a couple of clarifying questions directly in the email. 'Classic,' Alexander said, showing me the correspondence. Alexander is a developer who searched for a job for over four months and learned to distinguish a bot from a human during that time. A bot replies immediately or late at night. A recruiter replies on the third to fifth day and writes differently: 'Alexander, good afternoon! I've reviewed your experience with high-load projects...' He gets responses to one or two out of ten applications, and in about seven out of ten cases, a bot is the first to respond. Marina, an analyst, speaks about the same issue more calmly. On one platform, her applications simply hang: 'Usually, nothing happens. Two years ago, there was no feedback, and now there isn't either – stability is the key.' Read more

item.title: [Translation] Teleoperation, Simulations, and Cap Cams: How Data is Collected for Robot Training
item.description:
Language models have become much smarter due to scale, trained on trillions of text tokens. Robotics lacks this scale; millions of hours of robots folding shirts or pouring water haven't been uploaded. Each hour must be recorded from scratch. This article explores how robot training data is currently collected, how much has been gathered, and the cost of catching up to LLMs. By rough estimates, robots have about a thousand times less data. item.title: Two Claude Code accounts on one machine
item.description:
I have two Claude accounts. The first is corporate. The second is personal, I pay for it myself and use it in my projects. Both run on the same machine, and it quickly became clear that they should be kept separate. There are several reasons. Work code should go through the work account because the company has its own rules for this. Conversely, I don't want to run my own projects at the employer's expense and leave them in the corporate history. You can switch manually via /logout and /login, but "is this life?". I wanted the account to be selected automatically, depending on which project I opened. It turned out to be very easy to do. Read more

item.title: How to Make Your First Code Version Disposable
item.description:
Authors: Kirill Goncharov, Sergey Adamov (BusinessPad) Imagine this situation. You've set up an AI agent and used it to build a new product in two weeks – for example, an order approval system. In it, a manager creates an order, a financier checks it, a supervisor approves it, and then delivery is initiated. The system works, and users can go through the entire process from start to finish. But suddenly, details emerge that were difficult to foresee: it turns out that before sending an order to the supervisor, an additional check is needed, and orders over 100,000 rubles must be confirmed by the director. You open the code to make these changes and face a problem. The requirement for mandatory approval of large orders by the director is written in three places at once: in the interface, the server-side, and the instructions for the AI agent. Moreover, the wording differs, and it's unclear which one is correct. If you change the limit in one place, the others will continue to function as before: the interface won't display a notification about approval by the new person, the server will allow a large order without the director, and the AI agent will prompt users with the old workflow. The more new requirements appear, the harder it becomes to understand where related rules are located, what needs to be changed, and whether this change will disrupt the work of other parts of the system. From this, it's often concluded that vibe-coding cannot be used to build serious products. I propose a fresh perspective – don't demand perfect code from the first version of a product, but instead, create a complete description of the service in parallel with development. I'll explain what it provides, how to create it, and where to store it. Read more

item.title: Top AI Models for Code and Website Generation: Testing with a Single Brief
item.description:
If you're not deeply familiar with frontend development and building a website from scratch, and you need a website, you might have considered AI as a tool. This can be a correct, efficient, and rational decision – but only if you correctly formulate the brief and choose the right model. After all, different tools bring the same landing page to a working state in different ways. In this article, we will conduct a practical test of tools on one specific brief. Our methodology does not claim to be scientific, as the result of a neural network's work is non-deterministic and varies from case to case. In this article, we will analyze the GPT-6, Claude 5.5, DeepSeek V4.1, Qwen 3.8, and GLM 5.3 models. We will also examine benchmark measurements, although the focus will be on our practical test. This article is not a top list, as each use case leads to its own requirements for the model, and an abstract best model will not always be in demand for your specific case with your requirements. Read more
